title: Research
text: My research is centered on explainable AI, mechanistic interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and language-model reliability.

title: Research
text:
Research agenda
I am interested in explanations as operational signals: not only as post-hoc descriptions for humans, but as measurable quantities that can improve AI systems.
Current directions:

detecting contextual hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation,
using model-internal features for evaluation and reliability,
controllable generation with masked diffusion language models,
explanation-based covariate drift detection,
interpretable NLP systems for information extraction and document understanding,
reliable AI workflows for science and industry.

title: Research
text:
PhD thesis
Beyond Human Interaction: Alternative Applications for Explanations (TU Berlin / DFKI, since 2023)
Traditional XAI produces explanations for humans to read. My thesis instead treats attribution methods (Integrated Gradients, ALTI, LRP, and mechanistic decompositions of the residual stream) as internal signals that an AI system can consume itself. It is organised around three questions:

Can explanations detect when the input distribution changes? Attribution patterns shift before performance drops, enabling label-free drift detection.
Can explanations improve retrieval in RAG systems? Token-level attribution for pairwise embedding similarity, and attribution-based reranking of retrieved documents.
Can explanations verify factuality? Tracking which source tokens influence each generated token to detect contextual hallucinations and attach citations.

title: Research
text:
Explainability as an engineering signal
A recurring theme in my work is that explanations can be used to improve AI systems, not only to explain them after the fact. This includes model monitoring, drift detection, model evaluation, and mechanistic diagnostics.

Collaboration interests

title: Projects
text:
Training-Free Character-Length Control in Summarization with Diffusion Language Models — EMNLP 2026
Summarization with a fixed character length matters for headlines, article previews, notifications, subtitles, and UI text, where output must fit an exact space. Autoregressive models struggle with precise character-length control: training-based methods need task-specific fine-tuning, and zero-shot prompting only achieves approximate compliance.
DELTA (Diffusion Expected Length Targeting Algorithm) is a training-free, inference-time method for masked diffusion LMs. At each denoising step it estimates the expected character length of the output and dynamically inserts or removes masked positions to steer toward the target length. It requires no fine-tuning and works with off-the-shelf masked diffusion LMs (e.g. LLaDA, Dream).
Across three summarization benchmarks, DELTA reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude compared to baselines while maintaining competitive summary quality in both automatic and human evaluation.

title: Projects
text:
Hallucination detection from model internals
Ongoing work on detecting contextual hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation from the model’s internal computation. When a language model answers from a retrieved document, its attention heads mix evidence from the context with evidence from the model’s own self-generated tokens. Separating these contributions inside the residual stream yields signals of whether a generated answer is actually supported by the source, both as a training-free groundedness readout and as a supervised hallucination detector.

Why it matters
For scientific and high-stakes RAG systems, the practical question is often not only whether an answer sounds true, but whether each claim is grounded in the documents provided to the model.


Poster
This project was adapted into a collaboration-oriented poster for the AI Grid Summer School “AI for Science”, Paris 2026.

title: Projects
text:
GUARDRAIL
Grounded Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning with Deferrable, Reliable Abstention In LLMs
A Franco-German project proposal developed at the AI For Science 2026 Summer School (AI Grid · DataIA · SCAI), which I coordinate. Partners: DFKI Berlin, University of Bamberg (Cognitive Systems), Lamarr Institute / University of Bonn, Université Paris-Saclay, and INRAE MaIAGE.
Knowledge graphs enable symbolic fact-checking of LLMs, but current approaches assume the graph itself is reliable. When LLMs are used to build the graph, converting probabilistic outputs into discrete triples strips away the signal of how well each fact is supported by its source, so a KG can end up validating hallucinated claims instead of preventing them.
GUARDRAIL studies the end-to-end propagation of reliability signals in KG-grounded LLM reasoning for environmental data:

Uncertainty-aware KG construction — retain source-groundedness (from interpretability-based source attribution) and citation-network quality signals alongside each extracted triple.
Reliability-aware retrieval and claim verification — adapt graph-based retrieval and KG-grounded verification to use these signals, evaluated on climate-related claim verification (ClimateCheck).
Calibrated abstention — combine graph reliability, retrieval coverage, and model confidence into an answer-or-defer policy, with a secondary transfer to plant- and pest-related QA.

title: Projects
text:
Explanation-based drift detection
This work studies how explanation signals can be used to identify covariate drift. The motivation is to use interpretability methods as practical model-monitoring tools rather than only as human-facing explanations.

Entity linking for product carbon footprint estimation

title: Steffen Castle
text:
Research story


2019–2020
Improving neural network explanations
Master’s research on Pattern-Guided Attribution and Pattern-Guided Integrated Gradients.


2021
Using explanations for drift detection
Explanation signals as operational tools for detecting covariate shift.


2023
PhD: machine-internal uses of explainability
Thesis topic Beyond Human Interaction: Alternative Applications for Explanations. Rather than producing explanations for people to read, the thesis asks whether attribution signals can serve AI systems directly: detecting distribution shift, improving retrieval, and verifying factuality.


2024–2025
Explaining embedding similarity for retrieval
Adapting attribution methods (ALTI, Integrated Gradients) to pairwise embedding similarity, and using token-level attributions to rerank retrieved documents for RAG.


2025–2026
Hallucination detection from model internals
Separating context-derived from self-generated contributions inside the model to detect unsupported RAG answers.


2026
GUARDRAIL: reliability-aware knowledge graphs
Franco-German AI for Science project on propagating source-reliability signals from KG construction through retrieval, claim verification, and abstention.


2026
Controllable generation with diffusion language models
DELTA: training-free character-length control for masked diffusion LMs (EMNLP 2026).
